questions.question: The nucleus of a plant cell is surrounded by a jelly-like substance called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**cytoplasm**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **cytoplasm** is a jelly-like substance present within the cell membrane and surrounds the nucleus of both plant and animal cells. It serves as the medium for the organelles and cellular processes. *Hence, the correct answer is cytoplasm.*
 
• It is a semi-fluid, transparent, and homogeneous substance that provides support to the cell's internal components and maintains the shape of the cell.
 
• The cytoplasm is composed of **water, salts, and various organic molecules**, including proteins and enzymes, which are essential for cellular metabolism.
 
• All the organelles of the cell, such as mitochondria, chloroplasts (in plant cells), and the nucleus, are suspended in the cytoplasm, ensuring their mobility and functionality.
 
• The cytoplasm also plays a critical role in cellular activities, such as **transporting nutrients, facilitating chemical reactions, and housing the cytoskeleton**, which helps maintain the structural integrity of the cell.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Functions of Cytoplasm:**

 
 
• The cytoplasm is responsible for holding all the components of the cell, including organelles, in place.
 
• It acts as the site for many metabolic activities, such as **glycolysis** and other enzymatic processes.
 
• The cytoplasm enables the exchange of materials between organelles, supporting cellular communication and transport.
 
• It helps in the movement of genetic material and organelles during cell division, such as during **mitosis** and **meiosis**.
 
 
 
• **Key Characteristics of Incorrect Options:**
 
 
• **Plastids:** Plastids are double-membrane organelles found exclusively in plant cells. They are responsible for photosynthesis (chloroplasts), storage (amyloplasts), or pigment synthesis and storage (chromoplasts). They are not jelly-like substances surrounding the nucleus.
 
• **Vacuoles:** Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs found in plant and animal cells. They play a role in storage, waste disposal, and maintaining turgor pressure in plant cells. However, they do not surround the nucleus.
 
• **Chloroplasts:** Chloroplasts are a type of plastid that contains the green pigment chlorophyll. They are the site of photosynthesis in plant cells and do not surround the nucleus.
 
 
 
• **Composition of Cytoplasm:**
 
 
• The cytoplasm consists of about **80% water**, making it a hydrophilic environment for biochemical reactions.
 
• It contains ions, nutrients, enzymes, and other molecules necessary for cellular processes.
 
• The cytoplasm is further divided into two components: **cytosol** (the fluid part) and the organelles suspended within it.
 
 
 
• **Importance in Plant Cells:**
 
 
• In plant cells, the cytoplasm connects adjacent cells through channels called **plasmodesmata**, allowing communication and transport of materials between cells.
 
• The cytoplasm also plays a role in the **movement of chloroplasts** to optimize light absorption during photosynthesis.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The cytoplasm is often confused with the cytosol. While cytoplasm refers to the entire content within the cell membrane, excluding the nucleus, cytosol is the fluid part of the cytoplasm.
 
• In plant cells, the large central vacuole takes up a significant portion of the cytoplasm, pushing the other organelles, including the nucleus, towards the cell membrane.
 
• The cytoplasmic streaming, also known as **cyclosis**, is a process where the cytoplasm circulates within the cell, aiding in the transport of materials and organelles.
 
• The cytoplasm provides a medium for the biochemical reactions necessary for the survival and functionality of the cell.

questions.question: In which year was the Hindu Succession Amendment Act implemented?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**In 2005**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Hindu Succession Amendment Act** was implemented in the year **2005** to amend the **Hindu Succession Act, 1956**.
 
• This Act aimed to provide **equal inheritance rights** to daughters in ancestral property, bringing gender equality in the distribution of property.
 
• The amendment abolished the concept of **Hindu joint family property**, allowing daughters to become **coparceners**, just like sons.
 
• The Act applied to the **Hindus**, including Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs, making it comprehensive in its scope.
 
• The **2005 amendment** was a landmark step in ensuring women's **property and inheritance rights** in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Provisions of the Hindu Succession Amendment Act, 2005:**

 
 
• The Act granted **daughters the right to be coparceners** in the ancestral property, making them equal in rights and liabilities as sons.
 
• Before the amendment, only male members of the family were considered coparceners in a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF).
 
• The Act was applicable to **self-acquired property** as well as ancestral property.
 
• It stated that a daughter has the same rights in the property **from her birth**, irrespective of whether she is married or unmarried.
 
• The amendment also ensured that women had an equal say in the **partition and management** of the property.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Amendment:**
 
 
• The Act was a significant move towards **gender equality** in property inheritance laws in India.
 
• It empowered women to claim their rightful share in ancestral property, ensuring their **financial independence**.
 
• It helped reduce the **discrimination** faced by women in patriarchal societies regarding inheritance rights.
 
 
 
• **Exceptions and Legal Clarifications:**
 
 
• The Act does not apply to **Muslims, Christians, Parsis, and Jews**, as they have separate personal laws for property and inheritance.
 
• Further clarifications were made in **2015** by the Supreme Court, stating that a daughter is entitled to equal rights in property regardless of whether her father was alive on the amendment date (2005).
 
 
 
• **Comparison with the Hindu Succession Act, 1956:**
 
 
• The original Act of 1956 did not grant daughters the status of **coparceners** and restricted their inheritance rights.
 
• The 2005 amendment removed these restrictions, making the law more **equitable** for daughters.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Hindu Succession Act, 1956** was part of the Hindu Code Bills introduced to modernize personal laws for Hindus in independent India.
 
• The **Hindu Succession Amendment Act, 2005** was aimed at addressing gender inequality in property inheritance and empowering women.
 
• The amendment applies to **ancestral property** and self-acquired property, ensuring a fair distribution of assets.
 
• As per the latest rulings, the amendment applies **retrospectively**, granting daughters equal rights regardless of the father's death.
 
• This landmark legislation has played a crucial role in promoting **social justice** and gender equality in India.

questions.question: Which of the following sites is the evidence of domestication of dogs in ancient India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Burzahom**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Burzahom**, an archaeological site located in **Kashmir**, provides evidence of the domestication of animals, including dogs, during the **Neolithic period.**
 
• Excavations at Burzahom have revealed **pit dwellings**, tools, and artifacts that indicate the presence of a settled agricultural community.
 
• Among the findings were skeletal remains of domesticated dogs buried alongside humans, showcasing their significance in the community.
 
• The site is dated to around **3000 BCE**, making it one of the earliest known instances of dog domestication in ancient India.
 
• Burzahom’s findings highlight the transition from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to settled agriculture, where animals like dogs were integrated into daily life for purposes such as security and companionship.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mehrgarh**:

 
 
• Located in present-day **Balochistan, Pakistan**, Mehrgarh is a **Neolithic site** dating back to around **7000 BCE**.
 
• It provides evidence of early agricultural practices and the domestication of animals like sheep, goats, and cattle, but not dogs.
 
• Mehrgarh is considered one of the earliest sites showcasing the transition to farming in South Asia.
 
 
 
• **Hallur**:
 
 
• Hallur is a **Chalcolithic site** in Karnataka, India, dated to around **1500 BCE**.
 
• It is known for its evidence of early iron tools and agricultural practices.
 
• There is no significant evidence of dog domestication at this site.
 
 
 
• **Payyampally**:
 
 
• Located in Kerala, Payyampally is an **Iron Age site** known for its megalithic structures.
 
• It provides evidence of advanced tools, burial practices, and agriculture but lacks indications of dog domestication.
 
 
 
• **Burzahom**:
 
 
• Burzahom is unique in its discovery of **human-dog burial practices**, highlighting the domestication and cultural significance of dogs.
 
• The site also features pit dwellings, stone tools, and evidence of early agricultural activities.
 
• It is located in the **Kashmir Valley** and dates back to the **Neolithic era** around 3000 BCE.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Dog domestication** is believed to have started around **15,000 to 40,000 years ago**, with genetic evidence tracing their origins to wolves.
 
• In ancient India, dogs were used for **security, hunting, and companionship**, as seen in archaeological findings.
 
• The burial of dogs alongside humans at sites like Burzahom signifies their cultural and emotional importance in early societies.
 
• Such practices indicate a shift towards recognizing animals as integral members of the community rather than merely utilitarian assets.
 
• Burzahom is a rare site in South Asia providing direct evidence of early dog domestication and its association with human settlements.

questions.question: Which of the following peaks of the Himalayas is in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kanchenjunga**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kanchenjunga** is the **third-highest peak in the world**, with an elevation of **8,586 meters (28,169 feet)**, and it is located in the Himalayan range along the border of **India** (Sikkim state) and Nepal.
 
• It is the **highest peak in India** and is considered sacred by the people of Sikkim.
 
• Unlike Mount Everest, Dhaulagiri, or Gurla Mandhata, **Kanchenjunga lies partially in India**, making it the correct answer for a Himalayan peak within India.
 
• The peak is part of the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area and is known for its **unique biodiversity** and **cultural significance**.
 
• Kanchenjunga is surrounded by five peaks, collectively known as the "Five Treasures of Snow" (referring to its sacred status in local beliefs).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mount Everest:**

 
 
• It is the **highest peak in the world**, standing at **8,848.86 meters** (29,031.7 feet).
 
• Located on the border between **Nepal** and the **Tibet Autonomous Region of China**, it is not in India.
 
• It is known as **Sagarmatha** in Nepal and **Chomolungma** in Tibet.
 
 
 
• **Gurla Mandhata:**
 
 
• It is located in **Tibet**, near the sacred Lake Manasarovar and Mount Kailash.
 
• Its height is **7,694 meters (25,243 feet)**, and it lies entirely outside India.
 
 
 
• **Dhaulagiri:**
 
 
• Dhaulagiri is the **seventh-highest mountain in the world**, with an elevation of **8,167 meters (26,795 feet)**.
 
• It is located entirely in **Nepal** and is known for its dramatic rise over the Kali Gandaki River.
 
 
 
• **Kanchenjunga:**
 
 
• Kanchenjunga is located in the eastern Himalayas, forming part of the **Sikkim Himalayas**.
 
• The peak lies on the border between **Sikkim (India)** and **eastern Nepal**. However, certain parts, such as its southeastern and northeastern slopes, are in India.
 
• It holds **cultural and religious significance** for the local communities, especially the Lepchas, who consider it sacred.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Himalayan Peaks in India:**

 
 
• Besides Kanchenjunga, other significant Himalayan peaks located in India include **Nanda Devi**, **Kamet**, and **Trisul**.
 
• These peaks are located in regions like **Uttarakhand**, **Sikkim**, and **Arunachal Pradesh**.
 
 
 
• **Conservation Efforts:**
 
 
• The Kanchenjunga Biosphere Reserve in Sikkim is a UNESCO World Heritage Site recognized for its **rich biodiversity**.
 
• Efforts are underway to balance ecological conservation with tourism in the region.

__
 
• In **1651**, the first English factory in India was established on the banks of the **Hooghly River**, near the town of Hugli in Bengal.
 
• This marked the beginning of **English East India Company’s** commercial activities in Bengal. The factory served as a trading post for the company.
 
• The location was strategically chosen as the **Hooghly River** was a major waterway, facilitating trade and transport in Bengal.
 
• The establishment of this factory eventually paved the way for the **British colonial rule** in India, as the East India Company gained significant economic and political influence in the region.
 
• The factory primarily dealt in the trade of **silks, muslins, saltpetre**, and other goods that were in high demand in Europe.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The Role of Hooghly River:**

questions.question: Regional Rural Banks fall under which category of banks?

The correct answer is __**Commercial Bank**__.

__
 
• **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** are categorized as **Commercial Banks**. They are a part of the Indian banking system and were established to ensure rural financial inclusion by providing banking services to rural and semi-urban areas.
 
• RRBs were established under the **Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976**, with the aim to develop rural economies by providing credit and other financial facilities to small farmers, agricultural laborers, and rural artisans.
 
• RRBs operate under a **three-tier structure**, where they are jointly owned by the **Government of India (50%)**, the **respective State Government (15%)**, and a **sponsoring Commercial Bank (35%)**. This ownership structure ensures a blend of local and centralized management.
 
• Their primary objective is to provide financial assistance to the weaker sections of society, including small and marginal farmers, micro-enterprises, and rural entrepreneurs.
 
• RRBs are regulated by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and supervised by the **NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development)** to ensure their smooth functioning and alignment with national goals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Characteristics of Regional Rural Banks:**

 
 
• RRBs primarily cater to the **credit needs of rural areas**, focusing on sectors such as agriculture, trade, and small-scale industries.
 
• They are designed to provide **low-cost banking solutions** to rural populations, especially those who lack access to traditional banking services.
 
• RRBs have limited operational areas, typically confined to a few districts, to ensure a focus on regional development.
 
• They provide both **short-term** and **long-term loans**, along with deposit services, to support agricultural and rural development.
 
• RRBs were initially exempt from maintaining the **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** and **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)**, but now they are required to comply with these regulations like other Commercial Banks.
 
 
 
• **Functions of Commercial Banks:**
 
 
• Commercial Banks provide a wide range of financial services, including accepting deposits, offering loans, and facilitating transactions.
 
• They serve as intermediaries, channeling funds from depositors to borrowers, contributing to overall economic growth.
 
• Commercial Banks are regulated by the **Reserve Bank of India**, ensuring financial stability and compliance with banking norms.
 
• They operate under various categories, including **Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, Foreign Banks, and Regional Rural Banks**.
 
 
 
• **Other Types of Banks:**
 
 
• **Co-operative Banks:** These banks are owned and operated by members to provide financial services to a specific community or group. They operate under the **Co-operative Societies Act**.
 
• **Payments Banks:** These are specialized banks that provide basic banking services, such as deposits and remittances, but are not allowed to lend or issue credit cards. They were introduced in **2014**.
 
• **Small Finance Banks:** These banks cater to the underserved and unserved sections of the population, including small businesses, marginal farmers, and micro-enterprises. They are regulated by the **RBI**.

• **Zaid season** is a short cropping season in India that falls between the **Rabi** and **Kharif seasons**. It typically starts in March and ends in June.

• The Zaid season is characterized by the **availability of irrigation facilities**, as the crops grown during this period rely on artificial watering since the monsoon rains have not yet arrived.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• It is known for its high **water content**, making it a hydrating and refreshing crop during the hot Zaid season.

• This season primarily relies on **irrigation systems** since it occurs during the summer months when rainfall is minimal.
 
• Crops grown during the Zaid season are usually **short-duration and heat-tolerant**.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a source of fresh water?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ocean**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Freshwater sources** include rivers, lakes, ponds, and streams. These water bodies are characterized by low salt content (**less than 0.5% salinity**), making them suitable for drinking and irrigation.
 
• **Oceans** are not considered freshwater sources because they contain a high level of salinity (**approximately 3.5% salt**). This makes ocean water unsuitable for direct consumption or agricultural use without desalination processes.
 
• Rivers are important sources of freshwater and provide water for drinking, agriculture, industry, and hydroelectric power generation.
 
• Lakes, especially freshwater lakes, are natural reservoirs that store water for various uses such as drinking water supply, recreation, and ecosystem support.
 
• Ponds are smaller water bodies that often provide localized sources of freshwater, supporting biodiversity and small-scale irrigation.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Ocean.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rivers:**

 
 
• Rivers are flowing bodies of freshwater that often originate in mountains or hills and eventually drain into seas or oceans.
 
• They play a critical role in sustaining human life by providing water for consumption, irrigation, navigation, and energy generation.
 
• Examples of major rivers include the **Amazon, Nile, Ganges, and Mississippi Rivers.**
 
 
 
• **Lakes:**
 
 
• Lakes are large standing bodies of freshwater surrounded by land.
 
• They serve as natural reservoirs, controlling floods, supporting aquatic ecosystems, and providing water for nearby communities.
 
• Examples include **Lake Superior, Lake Victoria, and Lake Baikal.**
 
 
 
• **Ponds:**
 
 
• Ponds are smaller and shallower water bodies compared to lakes.
 
• They support localized ecosystems, provide water for irrigation, and serve as habitats for diverse flora and fauna.
 
• Ponds are often artificial, created for agricultural purposes or as decorative features.
 
 
 
• **Oceans:**
 
 
• Oceans cover approximately **71% of the Earth's surface** and contain saline water.
 
• Desalination plants are required to convert ocean water into potable water, which is an energy-intensive process.
 
• Major oceans include the **Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic Oceans.**
 
 
 
• **Freshwater vs. Saltwater:**
 
 
• Freshwater contains minimal salt (**less than 0.5% salinity**), while saltwater, such as that found in oceans, has higher salinity levels (**around 3.5% salinity**).
 
• Freshwater is essential for human consumption, agriculture, and industrial use, whereas saltwater requires desalination for similar purposes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Global Freshwater Availability:**

 
 
• Freshwater constitutes only **2.5% of Earth's total water**, with most of it locked in glaciers and ice caps.
 
• Accessible freshwater from rivers, lakes, and groundwater accounts for less than **1% of Earth's water.**
 
 
 
• **Desalination:**
 
 
• Desalination is the process of removing salts and minerals from saline water to produce freshwater.
 
• This technology is widely used in arid regions like the **Middle East** and parts of **North Africa.**
 
• It is energy-intensive and expensive compared to using natural freshwater sources.
 
 
 
• **Conservation of Freshwater:**
 
 
• Freshwater conservation is critical due to increasing demands from agriculture, industry, and domestic consumption.
 
• Methods like rainwater harvesting, efficient irrigation techniques, and wastewater recycling help preserve freshwater resources.

• The **Subsidiary Alliance** system was a political strategy introduced by **Lord Wellesley**, the Governor-General of India, during his tenure from **1798 to 1805**.
 
• The system required Indian princely states to accept a British resident in their courts and maintain British troops at their expense, effectively reducing their sovereignty.
 
• Awadh, one of the major princely states, was forced to accept the Subsidiary Alliance in **1801**, under the pretext of providing protection and maintaining order.
 
• By **1856**, the British East India Company, under **Lord Dalhousie**, annexed Awadh into British India citing misgovernance, thereby removing the Subsidiary Alliance arrangement in the region.
 
• The annexation of Awadh in **1856** played a significant role in the unrest leading to the **Indian Revolt of 1857**, as it alienated local rulers and citizens.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Subsidiary Alliance:**

 
 
• Introduced by **Lord Wellesley**, the system aimed to expand British influence in India without direct annexation.
 
• States under the alliance had to maintain a British force and pay for its upkeep, or cede territory in lieu of financial support.
 
• It effectively reduced the power of Indian rulers, as they were not allowed to form alliances or declare war without British consent.
 
• Major states that accepted the alliance include **Hyderabad**, **Mysore**, **Tanjore**, and **Awadh**.
 
 
 
• **Annexation of Awadh:**
 
 
• Awadh was annexed in **1856** under the policy of **Doctrine of Lapse** and allegations of misgovernance.
 
• Its last ruler, **Nawab Wajid Ali Shah**, was dethroned, and the kingdom was brought under direct British control.
 
• The annexation disrupted traditional governance and economic systems, leading to widespread resentment among the people.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Subsidiary Alliance:**
 
 
• The alliance paved the way for British dominance over Indian princely states, making them dependent on British military and administrative support.
 
• It was instrumental in establishing British supremacy in India, but also caused dissatisfaction among Indian rulers and subjects.
 
• This dissatisfaction contributed to the buildup of resistance, culminating in the **1857 Revolt**.
 
 
 
• **Indian Revolt of 1857:**
 
 
• The annexation of Awadh and other princely states under policies like Subsidiary Alliance and the Doctrine of Lapse were among the key causes of the revolt.
 
• The revolt marked the first significant challenge to British rule, involving widespread participation from soldiers, peasants, and displaced rulers.
 
• The revolt led to changes in British policies, including the abolition of the East India Company and direct governance of India by the British Crown.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Doctrine of Lapse:**

 
 
• This policy was used by the British to annex Indian states where rulers died without a direct heir.
 
• Prominent states annexed under this policy included **Satara**, **Jhansi**, and **Nagpur**.
 
• The policy was introduced by **Lord Dalhousie**, further fueling resentment among Indian rulers.
 
 
 
• **Lord Dalhousie:**
 
 
• He served as the Governor-General of India from **1848 to 1856**.
 
• His policies of annexation and modernization, including railways and postal systems, had long-term impacts on India.
 
• However, his aggressive expansionist policies contributed to the unrest leading to the **1857 Revolt**.
 
 
 
• **British Governance Post-1857:**
 
 
• After the revolt, the British Crown took direct control of India, marking the beginning of the **British Raj**.
 
• The Governor-General was replaced by a **Viceroy**, representing the British monarch in India.
 
• Policies became more cautious, focusing on maintaining stability and preventing further revolts.

questions.question: Which of the following does not come in the Concurrent List of the Government?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Irrigation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Concurrent List** in the Constitution of India contains subjects on which both the **Union** and **State Governments** can legislate. However, in case of conflict, the Union law prevails.
 
• **Acquisition** refers to the process of acquiring property for public purposes and is listed under the Concurrent List. ***Hence, this statement is correct.***
 
• **Education** was transferred to the Concurrent List through the **42nd Amendment Act of 1976**. This allows both the Union and State Governments to make laws on education. ***Hence, this statement is correct.***
 
• **Forests** also fall under the Concurrent List, allowing joint governance for their preservation and management. ***Hence, this statement is correct.***
 
• **Irrigation** is a **State List subject** as per the Indian Constitution. It is primarily managed and legislated by State Governments. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• It divides the legislative powers between the **Union** and **State Governments** into three lists: Union List, State List, and Concurrent List.
 
• The **Union List** contains subjects of national importance (e.g., defence, foreign affairs). Only the Union Government can legislate on these subjects.
 
• The **State List** contains subjects of local or state importance (e.g., police, public health). Only State Governments can legislate on these subjects.
 
• The **Concurrent List** includes subjects of common interest to both the Union and State Governments (e.g., education, marriage, and bankruptcy).
 
 
 
• **Forests in the Concurrent List:**
 
 
• Forests were originally part of the State List but were moved to the Concurrent List by the **42nd Amendment Act of 1976**.
 
• This change was made to ensure uniform policies for forest conservation and management across India.
 
• Both the Union and State Governments now share responsibility for legislation and implementation regarding forests.
 
 
 
• **Education in the Concurrent List:**
 
 
• Education was also shifted to the Concurrent List by the **42nd Amendment Act of 1976**.
 
• This shift allows the Union Government to play a greater role in developing national education standards and policies.
 
• The change has facilitated large-scale national initiatives like the **Right to Education Act, 2009**.
 
 
 
• **Irrigation as a State Subject:**
 
 
• Irrigation is a subject under the **State List**, meaning that state governments have the primary authority to legislate and manage it.
 
• States undertake irrigation projects, manage water resources, and regulate their use within their boundaries.
 
• Examples include major irrigation projects like the **Bhakra Nangal Dam** in Punjab and the **Hirakud Dam** in Odisha, which are managed at the state level.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **42nd Amendment Act of 1976:**

 
 
• This amendment is considered the most comprehensive revision of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It transferred several subjects, including **Education**, **Forests**, and **Weights and Measures**, from the State List to the Concurrent List.
 
• The change aimed to strengthen the role of the Union Government in addressing issues of national importance.
 
 
 
• **Water Management and Irrigation:**
 
 
• While irrigation is a State Subject, inter-state river disputes are addressed under the Union List (e.g., **Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956**).
 
• The Union Government intervenes only in cases of disputes between states regarding river water sharing.

questions.question: Which of the following is a folk musical instrument played during Bhangra in Punjab?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tumbi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tumbi** is a traditional folk musical instrument of Punjab, India, and is widely used in performing Bhangra, a popular and energetic dance form of the state.
 
• The Tumbi is a **single-string plucked instrument** and is known for its high-pitched and rhythmic sound, which perfectly complements the lively beats of Bhangra music.
 
• This instrument is made using natural materials like a **wooden stick** for the neck and a **resonator made of a dried gourd or wood**. A metallic string is attached to it, which is plucked to produce sound.
 
• It is simple in design and construction but plays a significant role in traditional Punjabi music, especially during festive occasions and celebrations.
 
• The Tumbi has been popularized by Punjabi folk musicians and has also been incorporated into modern Punjabi pop and Bhangra music.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chikara**:

 
 
• The Chikara is a bowed string instrument used in folk music, particularly in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. While it is a folk instrument, it is not traditionally associated with Bhangra music in Punjab.
 
• This instrument has two main strings and is played with a bow. Its sound is deeper and more melodic compared to the Tumbi.
 
 
 
• **Sarinda**:
 
 
• Sarinda is a traditional stringed instrument used in various Indian folk music traditions, including in Punjab. It is played with a bow and has a hollow body resembling a lute.
 
• Although used in Punjabi folk music, it is not as prominently linked to Bhangra as the Tumbi.
 
 
 
• **Sambal**:
 
 
• Sambal is a percussion instrument commonly used in Maharashtra’s folk music, especially Lavani performances. It consists of two drum pieces that are struck together to produce rhythmic beats.
 
• It is not associated with Punjab or Bhangra music.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Bhangra Music:**
 
 
• Bhangra music combines traditional instruments like the Tumbi, Dhol, Chimta, Algoza, and modern instruments to create energetic rhythms.
 
• It plays a crucial role in celebrations like harvest festivals, weddings, and cultural events in Punjab.
 
• Modern adaptations of Bhangra music have gained international recognition, incorporating elements of pop and hip-hop music.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Tumbi** is highly regarded as a symbol of Punjabi musical heritage and is often featured in Bhangra performances to maintain its traditional essence.
 
• Prominent Punjabi artists, such as **Lal Chand Yamla Jatt**, have contributed significantly to popularizing the Tumbi through their music.
 
• While other instruments like the **Chimta** and **Algoza** also accompany Bhangra music, the Tumbi remains the most iconic instrument due to its unique sound.

questions.question: Who among the following is the head of the Government of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Prime Minister of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Prime Minister of India** is the head of the government and holds the most powerful executive position in the Indian political system.
 
• The Prime Minister is appointed by the **President of India** and is usually the leader of the party or coalition that has a majority in the Lok Sabha (the lower house of Parliament).
 
• The Prime Minister serves as the chief advisor to the President, is the head of the Council of Ministers, and plays a key role in formulating and executing government policies.
 
• Under the Indian parliamentary system, the Prime Minister has the authority to allocate portfolios to ministers, lead cabinet meetings, and represent the country in international forums.
 
• The position of Prime Minister was established under the provisions of the **Constitution of India**, which came into effect on **26th January 1950**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role and Responsibilities of the Prime Minister:**

 
 
• The Prime Minister is the chief decision-maker in the government and coordinates the functioning of various ministries and departments.
 
• He/she is the principal spokesperson of the government and represents India in diplomatic and international matters.
 
• The Prime Minister also plays a key role in legislative functions, including introducing bills and policies in Parliament.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Positions:**
 
 
• **President of India:** The President is the ceremonial head of state and acts on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.
 
• **Governor:** A Governor is the constitutional head of a state, and their role is limited to the state level.
 
• **Vice President:** The Vice President serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha (upper house of Parliament) but has limited executive powers.
 
 
 
• **Notable Prime Ministers in Indian History:**
 
 
• **Jawaharlal Nehru:** The first Prime Minister of India, who served from 1947 to 1964.
 
• **Indira Gandhi:** The first female Prime Minister of India, known for her strong leadership.
 
• **Narendra Modi:** The current Prime Minister (as of 2023), who has introduced several transformative policies and reforms.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Articles Related to the Prime Minister:**
 
 
• **Article 75:** Provides for the appointment of the Prime Minister and other ministers.
 
• **Article 78:** Specifies the duties of the Prime Minister in communicating with the President about decisions of the Council of Ministers.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Prime Minister's Tenure:** There is no fixed term for the Prime Minister, but they serve as long as they have the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
 
• **Eligibility:** To become the Prime Minister, a person must be a member of either the Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha and meet the qualifications for membership of Parliament.
 
• **Oath of Office:** The Prime Minister takes an oath of office and secrecy administered by the President of India.
 
• **Significant Powers:** The Prime Minister has the authority to recommend the dissolution of the Lok Sabha to the President and call for fresh elections.

questions.question: ______ can be described as infant mortality rate.

options.text: Deaths of children under one year of age per 1000 live births
Deaths of children under two years of age per 50 people

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Deaths of children under one year of age per 1000 live births**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **infant mortality rate (IMR)** is defined as the number of deaths of children under **one year of age** per **1000 live births** in a given year or region.
 
• IMR is considered a crucial indicator of a country's **healthcare system's efficiency** and the **overall development** of its population.
 
• The calculation of IMR involves dividing the **number of infant deaths** by the total number of live births, multiplied by 1000.
 
• The focus on children under one year is essential because this period is the most vulnerable due to **high susceptibility to infections, malnutrition, and birth complications**.
 
• IMR statistics are widely used in **policymaking**, especially for improving maternal and child healthcare programs globally and nationally.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Factors affecting Infant Mortality Rate:**

 
 
• **Healthcare access:** Limited access to healthcare facilities increases infant mortality.
 
• **Malnutrition:** Poor maternal and infant nutrition are significant contributors to infant deaths.
 
• **Infectious diseases:** Diseases like pneumonia, diarrhea, and malaria are leading causes of infant deaths.
 
• **Socio-economic factors:** Poverty, low education levels, and lack of sanitation directly impact IMR.
 
 
 
• **Global statistics:**
 
 
• According to the **World Health Organization (WHO)**, the **global IMR** dropped from 65 deaths per 1000 live births in 1990 to **29 deaths per 1000 live births in 2020**.
 
• Regions like **Sub-Saharan Africa** and **South Asia** still report high IMR due to healthcare disparities.
 
 
 
• **India's Scenario:**
 
 
• As per the **Sample Registration System (SRS) 2020**, India's national IMR was **28 deaths per 1000 live births**.
 
• States like **Kerala** and **Tamil Nadu** have the lowest IMR due to better healthcare infrastructure, while **Bihar** and **Uttar Pradesh** report higher IMR.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives to Reduce IMR:**
 
 
• **Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY):** Aimed at promoting institutional deliveries to reduce infant and maternal mortality.
 
• **Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS):** Provides nutritional support and healthcare to children under six years.
 
• **National Health Mission (NHM):** Focuses on improving maternal and child health outcomes in India.

• **The Chambal River** is not a tributary of the Ganga. It is a major tributary of the Yamuna River, which itself is a significant tributary of the Ganga.

• The **Gandak River** is a northern tributary of the Ganga, originating in Nepal and flowing through Bihar before merging with the Ganga.
 
• The **Alaknanda River** is a significant tributary of the Ganga in Uttarakhand and merges with the Bhagirathi at Devprayag to form the Ganga.
 
• The **Kosi River**, originating from the Himalayas in Nepal, is another tributary of the Ganga, known for its frequent changes in course and devastating floods.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• Originates from **Janapav Hills** in the Vindhya Range in Madhya Pradesh.
 
• Flows through **Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh**.

• **Kosi River:**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Ganga River Basin** is the largest river basin in India, covering significant parts of northern and eastern India.
 
• The **major tributaries** of the Ganga include the Yamuna, Son, Gandak, Kosi, Ghaghara, and Gomti rivers.
 
• The Ganga plays a vital role in **religion, economy, and ecology** in India, supporting millions of people in its basin.

questions.question: Which of the following is used to focus the rays of the Sun in a solar cooker to achieve a higher temperature?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mirror**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Mirrors** are used in solar cookers to focus the Sun’s rays onto a specific point, increasing the intensity of the heat and achieving higher temperatures.
 
• A concave mirror, in particular, is commonly used because it reflects and converges the Sun's rays to a focal point, concentrating the heat energy.
 
• Solar cookers with mirrors are designed to trap heat in an insulated cooking area, allowing food to cook effectively using only solar energy.
 
• This method is highly efficient and environmentally friendly as it utilizes renewable energy and does not produce harmful emissions.
 
• Mirrors in solar cookers are typically coated with reflective materials, such as aluminum or silver, to maximize the reflection of sunlight.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other Optical Devices:**

 
 
• **Prism:** A prism is a transparent optical element that refracts light. It is used for light dispersion and splitting white light into its constituent colors, not for focusing sunlight in solar cookers.
 
• **Convex Lens:** Convex lenses can focus sunlight to a point, but they are less commonly used in solar cookers due to their fragility and high cost compared to mirrors.
 
• **Concave Lens:** Concave lenses diverge light rays and are unsuitable for concentrating sunlight. They cannot create the focused heat required for cooking purposes.
 
 
 
• **Principle of Solar Cookers:**
 
 
• Solar cookers work on the principle of converting solar radiation into heat energy. The heat is then trapped within the cooker to cook food.
 
• Mirrors or reflective surfaces are used to focus sunlight onto a cooking vessel, while insulated materials prevent heat loss.
 
• Transparent glass covers further enhance the heat-trapping mechanism by allowing sunlight to pass through but reducing heat escape.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Solar Cookers:**
 
 
• Solar cookers are widely used in rural areas and regions with high solar intensity as a cost-effective cooking solution.
 
• They help reduce dependence on fossil fuels and firewood, contributing to environmental conservation.
 
• Solar cookers are also used in educational demonstrations to promote renewable energy technologies.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Impact:**
 
 
• Using solar cookers reduces greenhouse gas emissions, as they do not rely on conventional energy sources like coal or gas.
 
• They promote sustainable living and help conserve natural resources, such as forests, by reducing the need for firewood.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Types of Solar Cookers:**

 
 
• **Box Cookers:** These use flat mirrors to reflect sunlight into an insulated box where food is cooked. They are simple and cost-effective.
 
• **Parabolic Cookers:** These use a parabolic-shaped reflective surface to concentrate sunlight to a single point, achieving higher temperatures compared to box cookers.
 
• **Hybrid Cookers:** These are equipped with mirrors and electrical heating elements for use during cloudy conditions.
 
 
 
• **Efficiency Factors:**
 
 
• The efficiency of a solar cooker depends on the intensity of sunlight, the quality of the reflective surface, and the insulation of the cooking chamber.
 
• Proper alignment of the mirror with the Sun’s position is crucial for maximizing heat concentration.
 
 
 
• **Global Usage:**
 
 
• Countries like **India, China, and Kenya** actively promote solar cookers for rural and off-grid areas to reduce energy poverty.

questions.question: How many rasas are there in Indian classical dance?
questions.solution:

__
 
• In **Indian classical dance** and drama, the term "Rasas" refers to the **nine basic emotions** or moods that are expressed through gestures, facial expressions, and movements.
 
• The concept of Rasas originates from the ancient Indian treatise on performing arts, the **Natyashastra**, written by the sage Bharata.
 
• The **Nine Rasas** are as follows: **Shringara** (love), **Hasya** (laughter), **Karuna** (compassion), **Raudra** (anger), **Veera** (heroism), **Bhayanaka** (fear), **Bibhatsa** (disgust), **Adbhuta** (wonder), and **Shanta** (peace).
 
• Each Rasa is associated with a specific **Bhava (emotion)** or a state of mind, which the performers evoke in the audience.
 
• The Rasas form the core of the aesthetic and emotional experience in **Indian classical dance forms** like Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Odissi, Manipuri, and others.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Detailed Description of the Nine Rasas:**

 
 
• **Shringara (Love or Beauty):** It represents romantic love, attraction, and beauty. It is considered the king of Rasas.
 
• **Hasya (Laughter):** It denotes humor and joy, evoking feelings of happiness and amusement.
 
• **Karuna (Compassion):** It symbolizes sorrow and compassion, often eliciting empathy and pity.
 
• **Raudra (Anger):** It showcases fury and rage, representing destructive emotions.
 
• **Veera (Heroism):** It reflects courage, bravery, and determination in the face of challenges.
 
• **Bhayanaka (Fear):** It embodies fear and anxiety, creating a sense of dread.
 
• **Bibhatsa (Disgust):** It portrays aversion and repulsion.
 
• **Adbhuta (Wonder):** It represents amazement and curiosity at something extraordinary.
 
• **Shanta (Peace):** It signifies tranquility and calmness, often seen as the ultimate Rasa.
 
 
 
• **Importance in Indian Performing Arts:**
 
 
• The Rasas are essential for evoking emotional responses from the audience and are the foundation of expressive storytelling in Indian art forms.
 
• They are extensively used in **classical dances** like Bharatanatyam, where performers use facial expressions (abhinaya) to depict different emotions.
 
• In **Kathakali**, Rasas are brought to life through elaborate makeup, costumes, and precise movements.
 
• These emotions are also pivotal in Indian classical music, theatre, and literature.
 
 
 
• **Natyashastra:**
 
 
• Written by the sage Bharata, the **Natyashastra** is an ancient text on performing arts that provides detailed guidelines on dance, music, drama, and aesthetics.
 
• It serves as the primary reference for understanding the theory of Rasas and their practical application in performances.
 
 
 
• **Modern Relevance:**
 
 
• The concept of Rasas continues to influence contemporary art forms, including cinema, where emotional engagement is crucial.
 
• Understanding Rasas aids performers in creating a deeper connection with their audience.

questions.question: The process of making yarn from fibres is called _______.

__
 
• **Spinning** is the process of converting fibers into yarn. It involves twisting fibers together to form a continuous thread, which can then be woven or knitted into fabrics.
 
• The process uses a spinning wheel, spindle, or modern spinning machines to draw out and twist the fibers.
 
• Spinning is essential as it provides the base material (yarn) for making textiles and garments. Without spinning, fabrics cannot be produced.
 
• This process is used for both natural fibers like cotton, wool, and silk, as well as synthetic fibers like nylon and polyester.
 
• Spinning is a key stage in the textile production process, and the quality of yarn directly affects the quality of the final fabric.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ginning:**

 
 
• This process involves separating cotton fibers from seeds. It is the first step after harvesting cotton but is unrelated to yarn production directly.
 
• Ginning prepares cotton for spinning by ensuring the fibers are clean and free from impurities.
 
• Example: Cotton ginning machines are widely used in agricultural and textile industries.
 
 
 
• **Knitting:**
 
 
• Knitting is the process of interlocking loops of yarn to create a fabric. It is a different method of fabric production, not related to spinning.
 
• Knitted fabrics are stretchable and used for making items like sweaters, socks, and t-shirts.
 
• Example: Knitting machines or hand knitting needles are used for this purpose.
 
 
 
• **Weaving:**
 
 
• Weaving involves interlacing two sets of yarns (warp and weft) at right angles to create fabric.
 
• It is another fabric production method but requires yarns, which are produced through spinning.
 
• Example: Woven fabrics like denim, canvas, and silk are widely used in clothing and home furnishings.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Spinning:**
 
 
• Spinning determines the strength, fineness, and durability of yarn, which impacts the final fabric quality.
 
• It is a crucial step in the textile industry, forming the foundation for all subsequent processes like weaving, knitting, and dyeing.
 
• India, as a leading textile producer, has a significant number of spinning mills contributing to its economy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Textile Industry in India:**

 
 
• India is one of the largest producers of cotton and jute in the world and has a significant presence in spinning and weaving industries.
 
• The Indian textile industry employs millions and contributes significantly to the country's exports and GDP.
 
• Advanced spinning technologies, such as rotor spinning and ring spinning, are widely used in modern mills to increase productivity and quality.
 
 
 
• **Fiber Types:**
 
 
• **Natural fibers:** Cotton, wool, silk, and jute.
 
• **Man-made fibers:** Polyester, nylon, acrylic, and spandex.
 
• Both types of fibers undergo the spinning process to create yarn for various applications.

__
 
• **Overgrazing** is a significant factor leading to **soil degradation**. When livestock graze excessively on vegetation, it removes protective plant cover, leaving the soil exposed to erosion by wind and water.
 
• It depletes the **nutrient content** of the soil, making it less fertile and reducing agricultural productivity over time.
 
• Overgrazing also causes **compaction of soil**, reducing its ability to hold water and air, which are essential for plant growth.
 
• This practice disrupts the natural regeneration of plants, leading to the **loss of biodiversity** and desertification in severe cases.
 
• Overgrazing is especially prevalent in regions with high livestock populations and low vegetation density, contributing to large-scale environmental degradation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Crop Rotation:**

 
 
• Crop rotation is a sustainable agricultural practice where different types of crops are grown sequentially on the same land to maintain soil fertility and reduce soil degradation.
 
• It enhances soil health by replenishing nutrients and reducing the risk of pests and diseases. *Hence, this does not cause soil degradation.*
 
 
 
• **Afforestation:**
 
 
• Afforestation involves planting trees in barren or deforested areas, which helps in preventing soil erosion and improving soil quality.
 
• It is a critical measure for combating desertification and restoring degraded land. *Hence, this does not cause soil degradation.*
 
 
 
• **Fertilizing:**
 
 
• Fertilizers are used to provide essential nutrients to the soil for plant growth. However, excessive or improper use of chemical fertilizers can lead to soil degradation by polluting the soil and water bodies.
 
• Organic fertilizers, on the other hand, improve soil structure and fertility. *Hence, fertilizing itself is not a direct cause of soil degradation unless mismanaged.*
 
 
 
• **Effects of Overgrazing:**
 
 
• Overgrazing is a major driver of desertification, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions.
 
• It leads to the destruction of natural vegetation, increased soil erosion, and a decline in the land's capacity to support life.
 
• Examples include the Sahel region in Africa, where overgrazing has significantly contributed to desertification.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD):**

 
 
• The UNCCD aims to combat desertification and mitigate the effects of drought through sustainable land management.
 
• It emphasizes the importance of addressing issues like overgrazing, deforestation, and unsustainable agricultural practices.
 
 
 
• **Soil Conservation Techniques:**
 
 
• Practices like contour farming, terracing, and agroforestry are effective in reducing soil erosion.
 
• Encouraging sustainable grazing practices can help prevent overgrazing and promote soil health.

questions.question: What is the dangerous disease in humans and cattle caused by bacteria called?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Anthrax** is a dangerous disease caused by the bacterium **Bacillus anthracis**. It affects both humans and cattle.
 
• The disease is primarily contracted through spores of the bacterium, which can survive in harsh environmental conditions for years.
 
• Anthrax can present itself in different forms in humans: **cutaneous (skin), inhalation, gastrointestinal, and injection anthrax**.
 
• Cattle often contract anthrax through contaminated soil, water, or feed, leading to severe outbreaks in agricultural areas.
 
• Anthrax is classified as a zoonotic disease, meaning it can be transmitted between animals and humans, making it a public health concern.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Symptoms in Humans:**

 
 
• **Cutaneous Anthrax:** Causes skin ulcers with black centers, typically appearing on exposed body parts.
 
• **Inhalation Anthrax:** Severe respiratory issues, fever, and chest pain; often fatal if not treated promptly.
 
• **Gastrointestinal Anthrax:** Results from ingestion of contaminated food; symptoms include nausea, abdominal pain, and severe diarrhea.
 
 
 
• **Symptoms in Cattle:**
 
 
• Sudden death in livestock is often the first sign of an anthrax outbreak.
 
• Cattle may show symptoms like fever, difficulty breathing, and bleeding from natural body openings before death.
 
 
 
• **Prevention:**
 
 
• Vaccination of cattle and humans in areas prone to anthrax outbreaks is effective in controlling the spread.
 
• Proper disposal of infected animals and decontamination of affected areas is crucial.
 
 
 
• **Treatment:**
 
 
• Anthrax in humans is treated using antibiotics like **ciprofloxacin**, **doxycycline**, or **penicillin**.
 
• Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent severe complications.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Anthrax has been used as a biological weapon due to its ability to spread easily and cause fatalities.
 
• Notable cases include the anthrax attacks in the **United States in 2001**, where anthrax spores were mailed to individuals, causing widespread panic.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Global Distribution:**

 
 
• Anthrax outbreaks are common in agricultural areas where livestock graze on contaminated soil.
 
• Countries like **India, Africa, Australia, and parts of the United States** report frequent cases.
 
 
 
• **Anthrax in Public Health:**
 
 
• It is listed as a **Category A bioterrorism agent** by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
 
• Global health organizations conduct surveillance and vaccination programs to mitigate its effects.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Advancements:**
 
 
• Studies are ongoing to develop improved vaccines and treatments for anthrax.
 
• Efforts are also made to understand the bacterium’s survival mechanism in soil to control outbreaks effectively.

• The **Khilafat Committee** was formed in **March 1919** in **Bombay**. It aimed to defend the position of the Ottoman Caliph, whose authority was being undermined after World War I.

• The Khilafat Movement was supported by prominent leaders like **Mahatma Gandhi, Maulana Azad, and Ali Brothers (Shaukat Ali and Mohammad Ali)**, showcasing Hindu-Muslim unity during the Indian freedom struggle.

• **Khilafat Movement:**

 
 
• The movement began in the aftermath of World War I (1914-1918), when the Ottoman Empire faced territorial losses and the position of the Caliph was weakened by British colonial policies.
 
• It was initiated by Indian Muslims who wanted to protect the Caliphate and ensure the Ottoman Empire's sovereignty.
 
• Though primarily a Muslim-led movement, it gained support from leaders like **Mahatma Gandhi**, who saw it as an opportunity to unite Hindus and Muslims in the struggle against British rule.

• **Ali Brothers:**

• They worked closely with other nationalist leaders to combine the Khilafat Movement with the Non-Cooperation Movement against British rule.
 
 
 
• **Non-Cooperation Movement:**
 
 
• Launched in **1920** under the leadership of **Mahatma Gandhi**, the movement aimed to achieve Swaraj (self-rule) by boycotting British goods, institutions, and practices.
 
• The Khilafat Movement merged with the Non-Cooperation Movement, creating a united front against colonial oppression.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• By **1924**, the movement lost momentum after the abolition of the Caliphate by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in Turkey.
 
• Despite its decline, the movement left a lasting impact on Indian politics, promoting Hindu-Muslim unity during its peak.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Indian Freedom Struggle:**
